definition.text: How far a person counts nature as part of who they are.

facts.text: It behaves like a personality trait, staying fairly stable over time and across situations, yet it can grow after time spent in nature.
Schultz split it into three parts: feeling at one with nature (cognitive), caring for nature (affective) and committing to protect it (behavioural).
People who feel highly connected to nature report higher psychological and social well-being.
It reliably predicts environmental behaviour: highly connected people are more likely to join environmental groups and call themselves environmentalists.
A meta-analysis confirmed its strong correlation with pro-environmental behaviour but found a weaker causal role than the correlations suggested.
Raising people's connection to nature may motivate ecological behaviour more effectively than laws and rules.
More nature exposure and easier access to city green space may raise well-being and ecological behaviour, which matters to planners.

definition.text: A 21-item questionnaire that measures how connected to nature a person feels as a lasting trait.

facts.text: At least seventeen scales measure nature connectedness; the most used are Nature Relatedness, Nature Connectedness and Inclusion of Nature in Self.
Its three subscales measure identifying with nature, concern about human effects on the environment, and comfort and wish to be in nature.
It shows good reliability, alpha = .87, and test-retest stability six months later, alpha = .85.

definition.text: The probable fall in people's direct contact with nature, which earlier studies link to effects on health and on care for the environment.

facts.text: One review concluded that within a generation children's lives have largely moved indoors, while childhood nature experience builds lifelong care for nature.
A global review found the evidence still too thin to judge how large or general the decline is.
Indoor lifestyles and growing screen time have cut human contact with nature.

title: Nature therapy

definition.text: A broad group of treatments, also called ecotherapy, that use time in nature to improve mental or physical health.

facts.text: Its forms include forest therapy, forest bathing (shinrin-yoku) and Sami Lok.
Japan's forestry ministry head Tomohide Akiyama popularised forest bathing in 1982 to get more people into forests.
Its effects are usually tied to the body's stress recovery, as contact with nature lowers cortisol and heart rate.
Qing Li's small trials from 2005 found that walking in a forest for a few hours a day raised natural killer cells by roughly 50 percent; urban walks had no such effect.
Contact with nature is associated with lower stress and fewer depressive symptoms.
It is cheap and accessible, needing only parks, community gardens or other public outdoor space.
Reviews find results vary with study design, many studies rely on self-reports, and the evidence is not yet enough for clinical guidelines or proof of cause.

contested_note: Reviews disagree on how strong the evidence is, with some calling results inconclusive and asking for larger randomized trials.

definition.text: Health-system programmes in which doctors or public agencies formally send people to spend time in nature.

facts.text: Canada lets physicians formally prescribe nature, and since 2019 UK general practitioners have referred patients to the NHS-funded Dose of Nature programme.
Dose of Nature claimed a 64% recovery rate for its first 1500 patients, against 50% for talk therapy.
Finnish researchers recommend about five hours a month in nature as preventive health care.

definition.text: The idea that humans have an inborn urge to seek connection with nature and other living things.

facts.text: Edward O. Wilson introduced and popularised it in his 1984 book Biophilia; Erich Fromm had first used the word.
It has been developed within evolutionary psychology: ancestors with closer ties to nature may have found food, water and shelter more easily.
Research suggests modern cities are poorly suited to minds that evolved in natural settings.
It is used to explain why people keep plants, care for animals and sometimes risk their lives to save them.
Conservationists worry that losing this connection could breed disregard for wild species and speed ecosystem loss, so reconnecting people with nature has become a conservation goal.
It inspires biophilic cities with more green space, which can also serve as wildlife corridors.

definition.text: A neuroscience model holding that human vision has adapted to process nature's fractal patterns, those that repeat at different scales, with ease.

facts.text: Clouds, mountains and trees are natural fractals.
People process fractals with a fractal dimension between 1.3 and 1.5 especially well, and viewing them lowers physiological stress and boosts thinking.
Designers add biophilic fractals to buildings because people spend 92% of their time indoors.

title: Indigenous kinship with nature
article: Biophilia hypothesis#Indigenous perspectives on the human-nature connection

definition.text: The view, common in many Indigenous cultures, that humans are part of the natural world and bound to it by kinship and reciprocity.

facts.text: Humans, animals, plants and soil are seen as depending on each other for survival and health.
It underlies traditional ecological knowledge, such as the controlled burns used by some Native American and Aboriginal Australian societies.
Indigenous and animist beliefs usually treat nature as sacred, and the Anishinaabe make offerings before harvesting wild rice.

title: Attention restoration theory

definition.text: The theory that time in nature, or even views of it, helps people recover from the mental tiredness caused by sustained deliberate focus.

facts.text: Stephen and Rachel Kaplan argued that busy modern settings tax directed attention, which can run down into attention fatigue.
Nature evokes soft fascination, effortless attention to gentle stimuli such as drifting clouds or flowing water, which lets the mind rest.
A restorative setting has four properties: being away, extent, compatibility and fascination.
It builds on William James's distinction between effortful voluntary attention and automatic involuntary attention.
Roger Ulrich's competing Stress Reduction Theory says nature's benefits come from emotional and physiological responses rather than cognitive ones.
